answer: Submarines dive by changing their buoyancy. On the surface they float because large main ballast tanks are full of air. To dive, the crew opens vents at the top of those tanks so the air escapes and seawater floods in through openings at the bottom. That makes the boat heavier than the water it displaces, so it sinks [1][2]. Once it's underwater, smaller tanks do the fine work. Water is pumped into or out of them to hold a steady depth, and moved between tanks at the front and back to tilt the nose up or down [1]. Moving fins called diving planes, or hydroplanes, on the bow or sail and at the stern also steer the boat up or down while it's under way, a bit like an airplane's wings [1][2]. A submerged sub never stays balanced on its own: the hull gets squeezed as it goes deeper, which changes its buoyancy, so the crew keeps adjusting the tanks and planes [1]. To surface, compressed air is blown into the main ballast tanks. It pushes the water out, the boat becomes lighter than the water around it, and it rises [2].
